title: The Sower, the Storm, Legion, and Two Daughters
summary: Jesus travels preaching with the Twelve and a group of women who support the mission from their own means. He tells the parable of the sower and explains that the seed is the word of God, received differently by different hearts. Then come four acts of power: he calms a storm, frees a man possessed by a legion of demons, heals a woman who touches his cloak, and raises the daughter of Jairus.
story: Luke has been showing who receives the kingdom and who rejects it. Now Jesus explains why the same message produces such different results, through a parable about soil. Hearing is the chapter's theme: the sower's word is heard in many ways, the lamp must be seen, and Jesus' true family are those who hear God's word and do it. Then Luke gathers stories that show Jesus' authority over every enemy of human life: the chaos of the sea, the demonic, chronic disease, and death itself. Faith and fear run through all of them, preparing for the sending of the Twelve in chapter 9.
historical:
Only Luke describes the women traveling with Jesus at this stage of the Galilean ministry and names Joanna and Susanna; Mark mentions women who had followed him in Galilee only when they appear at the cross (Mark 15:40-41). Mary Magdalene was probably from Magdala, a fishing town on the western shore of the lake. Joanna's husband Chuza managed Herod Antipas's household, which means the support for Jesus' mission reached into the tetrarch's court. Joanna and Mary will be among the first witnesses of the empty tomb (24:10). Later Western tradition identified Mary Magdalene with the sinful woman of chapter 7, but nothing in the text connects them.

The east side of the lake lay in the region of the Decapolis, a group of cities with a largely Gentile, Greek-speaking population, which explains the herd of pigs. The name of the place varies in the manuscripts and the Gospels: Gerasenes, Gadarenes (as in Matthew 8:28), and Gergesenes. Gerasa (modern Jerash) is over thirty miles from the lake and Gadara about six; many think the event took place near Kursi on the eastern shore, where a steep slope comes down near the water, and that the Gospels name the wider district. Matthew mentions two possessed men; Mark and Luke focus on one. The parallels to this chapter are Mark 4-5 and Matthew 8, 9, and 13.
cultural:
Farmers in Galilee sowed by scattering seed by hand, sometimes before plowing it in, so seed landed on footpaths, thin soil over limestone, and patches of thorns as well as good ground. A hundredfold harvest was extraordinary. Parables, short stories or comparisons drawn from daily life, were a familiar Jewish teaching form; they invited hearers to think and to decide.

Several of the chapter's figures lived at the edges of purity law. Tombs were unclean, and pigs were unclean animals under Leviticus 11. According to Leviticus 15:25, a woman with ongoing bleeding was ritually unclean, and anyone she touched became unclean until evening; twelve years of this would have cut her off from worship and much of normal life. The fringe of Jesus' cloak probably refers to the tassels that Numbers 15:38-39 commanded Israelite men to wear. A synagogue leader like Jairus was a respected layman who oversaw its services. Mourning in that culture was loud and public, sometimes with hired mourners, which is why a crowd was weeping at the house.
literary: The chapter has two halves. The first (1-21) is about hearing: the parable, its explanation, sayings on the lamp and on listening, and the redefinition of Jesus' family. The second (22-56) is a series of four miracles, rising in intensity from nature to demons to disease to death. Luke keeps Mark's technique of framing one story inside another: the raising of Jairus's daughter is interrupted by the healing of the woman, and the two share the number twelve (twelve years of bleeding, a girl of about twelve). Each healed person is restored to family or community. Jesus calls the woman “Daughter”, joining her to the family of those who hear and trust.

outline.t: The Twelve and the women who travel with Jesus
Why parables, and the sower explained
A lamp on a stand: take care how you listen
A woman healed by touching his cloak

doctrines.note: The seed is the word of God, and its fruitfulness depends on how it is heard. Revelation is given, but it can be snatched away, choked, or received shallowly; it bears fruit in those who cling to it and persevere.

Jesus asks the disciples in the storm where their faith is, tells the woman her faith has healed her, and tells Jairus to believe even after news of death. Faith is trust in Jesus that holds under pressure and waits for his word.
Jesus does not reject his mother and brothers, but he names a deeper kinship: those who hear God's word and do it. The community of disciples becomes a family that includes the formerly unclean.

words.note: Musterion, mystery or secret. In the New Testament it does not mean a puzzle but something of God's plan once hidden and now revealed to those he chooses. The secrets of the kingdom are given to disciples as gift, not reached by cleverness.

Hupomone, perseverance or patient endurance. Luke alone adds it to the explanation of the good soil: fruit comes by persevering. It names staying power under trial, the opposite of the rocky soil that falls away in testing.

Abussos, the abyss or bottomless deep. In the Greek Old Testament it translates the deep waters; in Jewish thought of the period it was also a place where evil spirits were confined, as in Revelation 20:1-3. The demons fear it because they know Jesus has power to send them there.

christ: The disciples' question in the boat is the chapter's question: “Who is this? He commands even the winds and the water, and they obey Him!” In the Old Testament it is God who rules the raging sea and stills its waves (Psalm 89:9, Psalm 107:29). The demons name Jesus Son of the Most High God and tremble. Power goes out from him when a desperate woman touches him, and his word calls a dead girl back to life. What sets him apart is not only power but the way he uses it: he stops to find a woman who hoped to go unnoticed, gives her public restoration and calls her daughter, and remembers that a girl just raised from death needs something to eat. He sends the freed man home to tell how much God has done, and the man tells how much Jesus has done: Luke lets the two statements stand side by side.

hard.q: Does Jesus tell parables to keep people from understanding?
hard.a: Verse 10 quotes Isaiah 6:9, where God sends Isaiah to a people who will hear without understanding. Read on its own, it can sound as if Jesus hides the truth to keep people out. Most interpreters read it in the light of the whole chapter and of Isaiah. Parables reveal and conceal at once: to those who come to Jesus and ask, as the disciples do in verse 9, they open up; to those who have already closed their hearts, they remain only stories, and that result is itself a form of judgment on refusal, as it was in Isaiah's day. Some stress God's sovereign purpose in this; others stress human responsibility, pointing to verse 18's warning to take care how you listen. The verses that follow, about a lamp that is meant to be seen and hidden things that will be disclosed, show that the goal of Jesus' teaching is light, not concealment.

questions: Which of the four soils best describes how you have received God's word in this season of your life, and what would it take to become good soil?
The woman wanted to be healed without being noticed, but Jesus called her out in front of everyone. Why might he have wanted her healing to be public?
The people of the region asked Jesus to leave after he freed the man, because they were afraid. What might we prefer to keep, even at the cost of sending Jesus away?
